table.text: The trial was reviewed and approved by the South Central-Berkshire Research Ethics Committee and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> High resolution HLA genotypes from each participant were incorporated to compute participant-level, HLA-matched T S breadth scores by querying a catalog of thousands of TCR sequences with established experimental or statistical restriction to specific HLA alleles (i.e., HLA-A, -B, -C, or -DRB1) or functional heterodimers (i.e., DQA1-DQB1 / DPA1-DPB1) (see Methods, Extended Data Fig. 1 ).

> Prior to booster vaccination (Day 0, COV-BOOST), HA-T S breadth levels from previously vaccinated participants were only slightly elevated (p < 0.0001) compared to naive repertoires, consistent with the contraction of T cell memory from the earlier vaccination.

> Six participants were excluded from downstream analysis because their sample sets possessed insufficient starting DNA material (flagged by Adaptive Biotechnologies' laboratory) or lacked minimal clonal overlap between timepoints, suggesting a sample labeling error.

> Participants had previously received two doses of either AstraZeneca ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (ChAd) symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection were evaluated using a calendar-stratified Cox proportional hazards model to account June and November vaccination start months.

> For IPW weighting, participants were grouped by general prime-boost vaccine modalities: (i) Adenovirus / Adenovirus, (ii) . mRNA / mRNA, (ii) Adenovirus / mRNA, (iv) mRNA / Adenovirus, (v) .

> All participants were retained and Day 14 HA-T S breadth was imputed for low-recovery samples.

Ethics approval statement:

> The trial was reviewed and approved by the South Central-Berkshire Research Ethics Committee and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.formatted: As expected, booster administration induced a significant increase in the median HA-T S breadth score, increasing from 1.9 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 1.1 ✕ 10 -4 -2.4 ✕ 10 -4 ) pre-boost to 5.0 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 3.6 ✕ 10 -4 -7.5 ✕ 10 -4 ) post-boost (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">2 A</ref> ).
table.header: Booster vaccination increases breadth of antigen-specific TCRs
table.expanded: As expected, booster administration induced a significant increase in the median HA-T S breadth score, increasing from 1.9 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 1.1 ✕ 10 -4 -2.4 ✕ 10 -4 ) pre-boost to 5.0 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 3.6 ✕ 10 -4 -7.5 ✕ 10 -4 ) post-boost (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Extended Data Fig. 2 A ).

table.formatted: Components of HA-T S breadth attributable to CD4 + and CD8 + receptors both significantly increased between pre-and post-boost repertoires, with a moderate rank correlation (ρ = 0.55, p < 0.0001) between the absolute participant-level changes in CD4 + and CD8 + T S breadth from Day 0 to Day 14 (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">2 B-D</ref>).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p ≥ 0.10", "p ≥ 0.059", "p < 0.5", 
"p < 0.05", "p < 0.01"), Text = c("In contrast, the analogous HLA-agnostic Adaptive Biotechnologies Spike breadth metric did not as well separate cases from non-cases at either timepoint in aggregate or by T cell subset (all p ≥ 0.10), with the strongest but still non-significant signal in Day 14 CD4+ breadth (p = 0.096).", 
"None of the HLA-agnostic TCR metrics robustly separated cases from non-cases at either timepoint (Extended Data Fig. 6 G-L,S-X, all p ≥ 0.059).", 
"Because relatively few vaccinated participants possessed each inferred HLA allele, we intentionally applied permissive enrichment criteria to maximize sensitivity and retain potentially informative sequences (odds ratio > 1; Fisher's exact test p < 0.5).", 
"Clonotypes were retained if they demonstrated both substantial expansion (fold change > 2) and statistical significant change in template counts (FDR-adjusted Fisher's exact test p < 0.05).", 
"To link these expansions to HLA-restricted responses, expanded clonotypes were only retained receptors if they could be assigned to a common HLA allele or haplotype through enrichment testing in the post-infection repertoires (p < 0.01)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 11 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: The trial was reviewed and approved by the South Central-Berkshire Research Ethics Committee and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency.
live_data_statements: High resolution HLA genotypes from each participant were incorporated to compute participant-level, HLA-matched T S breadth scores by querying a catalog of thousands of TCR sequences with established experimental or statistical restriction to specific HLA alleles (i.e., HLA-A, -B, -C, or -DRB1) or functional heterodimers (i.e., DQA1-DQB1 / DPA1-DPB1) (see Methods, Extended Data Fig. 1 ).

Prior to booster vaccination (Day 0, COV-BOOST), HA-T S breadth levels from previously vaccinated participants were only slightly elevated (p < 0.0001) compared to naive repertoires, consistent with the contraction of T cell memory from the earlier vaccination.

Six participants were excluded from downstream analysis because their sample sets possessed insufficient starting DNA material (flagged by Adaptive Biotechnologies' laboratory) or lacked minimal clonal overlap between timepoints, suggesting a sample labeling error.

Participants had previously received two doses of either AstraZeneca ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (ChAd) symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection were evaluated using a calendar-stratified Cox proportional hazards model to account June and November vaccination start months.
For IPW weighting, participants were grouped by general prime-boost vaccine modalities: (i) Adenovirus / Adenovirus, (ii) . mRNA / mRNA, (ii) Adenovirus / mRNA, (iv) mRNA / Adenovirus, (v) .
All participants were retained and Day 14 HA-T S breadth was imputed for low-recovery samples.

text.text: HLA-driven heterogeneity and limitations of live T cell functional assays routinely thwart assessment of cell-mediated immunity in vaccination trials.

To address this, we developed a T-cell receptor (TCR)-based measure of immunogen recognition and evaluated it in COV-BOOST, a third-dose COVID-19 vaccine trial, during the Delta and Omicron waves (2021-2022, United Kingdom).
We estimated HLA-aware Spike-reactive T cell (HA-T S ) breadth from participant HLA genotypes, TCRβ repertoires, and a novel SARS-CoV-2 Spike HLA-linked reference catalog.
Higher post-boost HA-T S breadth was associated with lower symptomatic infection risk (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.39-0.86).
This association persisted after adjustment for neutralizing antibody titers and IFN-γ responses.
Examination of HA-T S across prior studies showed that it reflects participant genotype, exposure intensity, and time from exposure to sampling.
These findings highlight the possibility that estimates of antigen-specific T cell repertoire breadth could serve as a correlate of protection to accelerate vaccine development.

Immunological memory from infection and vaccination has reduced the population-level burden of severe COVID-19, even as reinfection waves drive viral escape from common antibody neutralization sites [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Immunological memory from infection and vaccination has reduced the population-level burden of severe COVID-19, even as reinfection waves drive viral escape from common antibody neutralization sites <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Meta-analyses of vaccine efficacy show neutralizing antibodies (nAbs) correlate strongly with protection against early post-vaccination infections [4] [5] [6] [7] .

text.text: However, this humoral protection wanes over time, is strain-dependent, and may not fully explain observed levels of vaccine efficacy 6, 8, 9 .

text.text: Thus, T cell mediated immunity has been proposed as a complementary mechanism underlying lasting protection against disease progression and severe clinical outcomes [10] [11] [12].
text.formatted: Thus, T cell mediated immunity has been proposed as a complementary mechanism underlying lasting protection against disease progression and severe clinical outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Considerable evidence supports a role for cellular immunity in the control of SARS-CoV-2 infection in animal models and humans.

In B cell-deficient mice, T cells were sufficient to provide antibody-independent protection against severe SARS-CoV-2 disease 13, 14 , and robust anti-SARS-CoV-2 T cell responses have also been observed in humans with B cell immunodeficiencies 15 .

text.text: In pediatric cohorts, the magnitude of spike-reactive IFN-γ-and IL-2-producing T cells following vaccination has been inversely associated with the risk of symptomatic infection over subsequent months 16 , and a household exposure study reported that early induction of SARS-CoV-2-specific IFN-γ-secreting T cells was associated with reduced viral load and milder disease 17 .

text.text: Although T cell responses were not directly analyzed, an analysis of humoral correlates of protection in a phase 3 trial of an adenovirus vectored vaccine (AZD1222), observed substantial vaccine efficacy even among participants with low levels of measured neutralizing antibodies 6, 7 .

S vaccine early in the pandemic showed that a higher fraction of TCRs associated with SARS-CoV-2 Spike antigen, measured 29 days post-vaccination, was associated with a reduced risk of severe, but not mild, COVID-19 during a 200 day follow-up 18.

text.text: Despite these lines of evidence for the protective role of T cells against SARS-CoV-2, few human studies have directly linked features of vaccine-elicited T cell repertoires to subsequent risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection using longitudinal designs.

Assessment of vaccine-induced cellular immunity in large trials is complicated by HLA-driven heterogeneity in T cell responses, the cost of cryopreservation, and lab-to-lab variability in live-cell assays.
To address this, we developed an HLA-aware (HA) analysis of T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing to estimate the clonotypic breadth of immunogen recognition.
The approach utilizes a newly constructed catalog of spike-specific TCRs developed from public data sources, to tally matching TCRs from each participant's repertoire based on their HLA genotype.
Applying this approach to a subcohort of the COV-BOOST trial 19, 20 , we investigated the association between TCRβ repertoire diversity and the risk of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infection.
text.formatted: Applying this approach to a subcohort of the COV-BOOST trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20</ref> , we investigated the association between TCRβ repertoire diversity and the risk of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 breakthrough infection.

text.text: The subcohort comprised SARS-CoV-2-naive participants who had previously received two doses of either an mRNA or ChAdOx COVID-19 vaccines.
Participants subsequently received one of several booster vaccine regimens.

Here we report that greater diversity of spike-reactive TCRs in peripheral blood TCRβ repertoires was associated with a lower risk of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection over the nine-month follow-up period.

In light of the challenges in storing PBMCs and standardizing live-cell functional assays for assessing vaccine specific T cell responses in large clinical trials, we developed an HLA-aware TCRβ sequencing-based approach to estimate the breadth of immunogen recognition by SARS-CoV-2 spike-reactive T cells (T S ).

This metric, which we term HA-T S breadth, assesses the proportion of spike-specific T cells in a repertoire by tabulating weighted matches to an HLA-defined SARS-CoV-2 spike TCRβ catalog (see Methods) and dividing the number of matches by total number of unique clonotypes.

High resolution HLA genotypes from each participant were incorporated to compute participant-level, HLA-matched T S breadth scores by querying a catalog of thousands of TCR sequences with established experimental or statistical restriction to specific HLA alleles (i.e., HLA-A, -B, -C, or -DRB1) or functional heterodimers (i.e., DQA1-DQB1 / DPA1-DPB1) (see Methods , Extended Data Fig. 1 ).
text.formatted: High resolution HLA genotypes from each participant were incorporated to compute participant-level, HLA-matched T S breadth scores by querying a catalog of thousands of TCR sequences with established experimental or statistical restriction to specific HLA alleles (i.e., HLA-A, -B, -C, or -DRB1) or functional heterodimers (i.e., DQA1-DQB1 / DPA1-DPB1) (see Methods , Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> ).

text.text: Briefly, each HLA-compatible TCRβ match is assigned a weight between 0 and 1 to reflect the uncertainty in sequence-based matching relative to the TCRβ's baseline prevalence in HLA-matched SARS-CoV-2 naive repertoires; a weight close to 1 indicates high certainty that the detected TCRβ is spike-specific in that HLA-context, evidenced by its low prevalence in HLA-matched SARS-CoV-2 naive repertoires (see Methods).
We computed HA-T S breadth in paired pre-(Day 0) and post-boost (Day 14) repertoire samples for a subset of participants within the COV-BOOST trial (n = 120).

As expected, booster administration induced a significant increase in the median HA-T S breadth score, increasing from 1.9 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 1.1 ✕ 10 -4 -2.4 ✕ 10 -4 ) pre-boost to 5.0 ✕ 10 -4 (IQR: 3.6 ✕ 10 -4 -7.5 ✕ 10 -4 ) post-boost (p < 0.0001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Extended Data Fig. 2 A ).

text.text: Components of HA-T S breadth attributable to CD4 + and CD8 + receptors both significantly increased between pre-and post-boost repertoires, with a moderate rank correlation (ρ = 0.55, p < 0.0001) between the absolute participant-level changes in CD4 + and CD8 + T S breadth from Day 0 to Day 14 (Extended Data Fig. 2 B-D).

text.text: The greater sensitivity to detect more clonotypes via HA-T S likely reflects two aspects of our approach.

First, the new HLA-aware SARS-CoV-2 Spike catalog draws on experimental data from post-vaccine repertoires, which may be favorable for identifying Spike-specific responses given lack of competition with T cell responses to other viral antigens (e.g., epitopes in nucleocapsid protein or ORF1) seen in natural infection; second, our approach accommodates more ambiguous, higher probability of V(D)J-recombination sequences via confidence weighting and tabulates catalog hits only in participants carrying the corresponding HLA, potentially allowing more Spike-specific sequences to be included in the reference set.

Expected HLA-intrinsic breadth, based on HLA genotype alone, partially predicts clinical risk
We defined HA-T S breadth as the proportion of unique TCRs in a repertoire expected to recognize the spike antigen.

Because this metric relies on matching TCRs to a subset of the reference catalog defined by an individual's HLA genotype, the maximum measurable breadth is inherently linked to each person's specific HLA alleles and their catalog representation.

While the HLA-defined catalog may reflect biases in its curation, we hypothesized that the differences in the potential breadth scores associated with combinations of HLA alleles may reflect genuine biological differences in the presentation efficiency of distinct HLA proteins.

That is, if specific HLA variants poorly present vaccine or viral peptides, individuals carrying more weak-presenting alleles may mount a weaker T cell response overall and potentially face higher clinical risk.
It is also possible that the composition of HLA-defined catalogs could be influenced by observational bias.

For instance, highly prevalent HLA alleles afford greater statistical power for discovering public TCRs https://paperpile.com/c/1j42lF/n1yc , and experimental techniques like tetramer staining inherently bias libraries toward known class I presented epitopes.

text.text: First we consider an individual's expected HLA-intrinsic Breadth (E[HA-T S,HLA ]), which we simulated based on a participant's complement of class I (HLA-A, B, C) and class II (DRB1, DQA/B, DPA/B) alleles and the analogous allele-specific T S breadth contributions observed in independent cohort of individuals with a defined SARS-CoV-2 S vaccine exposure.

For each individual and their HLA genotype, we used Monte Carlo sampling across the relevant allele-specific components to simulate a potential distribution of expected breadth scores; we used the median score to represent their expected HLA-intrinsic spike reactive breadth E[HA-T S,HLA ].

We can then compute a residual breadth ratio (HA-T S / E[HA-T S,HLA ]), which is the ratio of observed to expected breadth; conceptually this captures whether an individual over-or under-performed the genetic baseline (Extended Data Fig. 8 ).

text.text: Despite this clear evidence for antigen exposure to drive observable T S after infection, we reasoned that a low E[HA-T S,HLA ] might predispose SARS-CoV-2 naive individuals to a poor initial T cell response at baseline, compromising immunological control.
Because acute phase repertoires (direct measures of HA-T S after infection) reflect sample timing and intensity of disease course, they therefore are suboptimal for predicting risk.
However, we hypothesized that the expected HLA-intrinsic breadth (E[HA-T S,HLA ] ), which is based on genotype information alone, might reflect early T cell response capacity.

text.text: In this study, we developed an HLA-aware catalog of spike-specific TCRs to quantify the diversity of individual T cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 following infection and vaccination.

The post-vaccination HA-T S breadth scores of individuals in the COV-BOOST study were associated with risk of symptomatic COVID-19, with above-median scores associated with approximately 3-fold lower risk independent of measured T cell function (ELISpot) and neutralizing antibody titer.

The catalog curation approach integrated TCRs with (i) experimentally validated specificity, or (ii) strong statistical associations across large cohorts with spike antigen exposure, conditioning to individuals with a predicted restricting HLA allele.
The resulting catalog contains thousands of TCRβ sequences recruited by HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DR, HLA-DQAB, and HLA-DPAB variants, which can be a resource to future studies of SARS-CoV-2 immunity.

Further investigation demonstrated that in addition to estimation of observed T S breadth scores, the catalog enables estimation of an individual's underlying capacity for spike-reactive T cell breadth based on their HLA genotype alone, generating hypotheses about the role of aggregate HLA variation in T cell mediated immunity.

The identification of reliable T-cell immune correlates of protection remains central to evaluating and optimizing next-generation vaccines and evaluating risk-level among populations with partial-T cell immunodeficiencies.
Although neutralizing antibody titers have served as valuable surrogates of protection against SARS-CoV-2 and other pathogens 34 , they capture only one dimension of adaptive immunity.

text.text: T cells provide complementary protection against symptomatic and severe disease via cytotoxic elimination of infected cells and by supporting high-quality antibody affinity maturation 35.

text.text: Moreover, population level viral escape from T cell recognition is expected to occur more slowly than escape from neutralizing antibodies 36, 37 .

text.text: As viral evolution undermines the predictive value of pseudoneutralization assays against prior circulating strains, it is critical to determine whether blood-based T cell signatures can also serve as correlates of protection.
In this study, models incorporating HA-T S, or E[HA-T S,HLA ] predicted the risk of symptomatic infection after booster vaccination more accurately than Day 28 NT 50 antibody measurements alone.
However, this comparison is inherently constrained by the timing of antibody sampling.

While the available Day 28 NT 50 measurement may represent peak neutralization titers against ancestral strains, it may not fully capture antibody durability or cross-neutralization potency against the circulating Delta and Omicron variants.
Thus, the association between HA-T S breadth and lower symptomatic infection risk may reflect a direct, cytotoxic layer of T cell-mediated protection.
Alternatively, HA-T S breadth might also serve as a second-order biomarker for the quality and persistence of the humoral response that is not fully reflected in the Day 28 NT 50.

Recent data highlight that decay rates of anti-S antibody vary between individuals 38 ; for example, Park et al. (2025) found that the risk of breakthrough infection was actually highest among individuals with high initial post-booster anti-S IgG titers but rapid antibody decay kinetics, rendering single-point anti-S IgG measurements insufficient to predict risk 39 .

(2025) found that the risk of breakthrough infection was actually highest among individuals with high initial post-booster anti-S IgG titers but rapid antibody decay kinetics, rendering single-point anti-S IgG measurements insufficient to predict risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">39</ref> .

text.text: Interestingly, while anti-S IgG and ELISpot metrics measured after vaccination failed to predict infection outcome in that study, Park and colleagues noted that anti-S IgA levels on Day 28 did correlate with protection.

Thus, if post-boost SARS-CoV-2 S reactive T cell diversity reflects a well coordinated immune response that supports antibody class switching, affinity maturation, or sustained antibody production, then the protection we observed after vaccination could -at least in part -be antibody-mediated, yet statistically linked to higher levels of HA-T S cell breadth post-boost.

Weighing the roles of these two feasible mechanisms of protection will therefore require longitudinal antibody profiling alongside T cell sequencing to test whether post-boost acquired T S cell breadth is linked with differential antibody quality or decay kinetics.

A functional measure of T cell response (ELISpot), which was correlated with HA-T S,CD8+ breadth but not HA-T S,CD4+ breadth in this study, also predicted a reduction in symptomatic infection risk after booster vaccination.
This aligns with direct protection from enhanced cellular mediated immunity, since persons who can mount robust post-infection effector T cell response tend to have better disease outcomes 17,33   ).
Nonetheless, the magnitude of initial Spike-specific T cell IFN-γ response may only partially predict the durability and polyfunctionality of T cell memory.

Additional signs of a robust spike-reactive clonal diversity, captured by TCR sequencing, could encompass a wider range of receptor affinities beneficial for T cell survival in germinal centers or sustained tissue-resident immunity, consistent with a prior study showing that SARS-CoV-2 T cell clonal diversity, rather than individual clonotype abundance in blood, better predicted persistence of cellular memory 40.

text.text: The primary study population in the COV-BOOST trial was drawn from multiple sites in the United Kingdom, enriched for so far well studied HLA alleles (e.g., A*02:01, A*03:01, B*08:01), which increases the chance that the SARS-CoV-2 S reactive catalog developed in this study matched vaccine elicited receptors.

Although this cohort was not large enough to definitively assess whether risk of symptomatic breakthrough infection varied due to carriership of single HLA variants, it was notable that fewer symptomatic infections were observed in individuals carrying HLA-A*03:01, the second best represented class I allele in the newly developed HLA SARS-CoV-2 S catalog, with over 400 reference receptors.

The robust contribution of A*03:01-linked receptors to E[HA-T S ] breadth is consistent with the hypothesis that specific HLA alleles that activate diverse vaccine acquired CD8 + T cells may enhance effective immunological control [40] [41] [42] .

text.text: The methodology employed in this study to generate an HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2 spike catalog integrated data from multiple data sets benefited from unprecedented immunological data collection that occurred during the SAR-CoV-2 pandemic.

Based on sample availability, we analyzed a set of participants with paired Day 0 and Day 14 PBMC samples for TCR sequencing and functional assays.
Cases were determined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test (e.g.,an antigen detection or nucleic acid amplification test) starting 1 week after vaccination.
Non-case controls were participants with no evidence of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection through the end of April 2022.
Based on sample availability, controls were selected from eligible non-cases in proportion to the treatment assignment of the cases.
From available samples, one male and one female non-case participant of similar age was selected for every case.
After sample processing, the final dataset comprised 120 participants (43 cases and 77 controls) with matched Day 0 and Day 14 TCR repertoires.
Participant HLA information was not considered in sample selection.
To construct a large catalog of HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2 Spike-reactive T cell receptors (TCRs), we integrated prior public data.
We considered evidence from cohort-wide statistical enrichment testing, longitudinal vaccination studies, and previously published experimental validation datasets.

Our objective was to maximize sensitivity for identifying candidate Spike-reactive clonotypes from bulk single-chain TCRβ data while preserving information regarding the strength evidence for TCRβ-antigen-specificity through sequence-level confidence weighting.
To identify novel HLA-associated TCRs induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection, we analyzed 1,355 TCR repertoires previously collected from individuals with acute and convalescent COVID-19 23, 52 .

Because the post-infection repertoires contained TCRs targeting multiple SARS-CoV-2 antigens, including likely immunodominant responses against the nucleocapsid and ORF1 proteins, we next sought to identify receptors likely reactive to the S protein found in current vaccines.

For each candidate TCR, we assessed enrichment among individuals carrying the predicted HLA-allele following vaccination.
A sequence was retained as putatively Spike-reactive if it was detected more frequently in HLA-matched post-vs. pre-vaccination repertoires.

Because relatively few vaccinated participants possessed each inferred HLA allele, we intentionally applied permissive enrichment criteria to maximize sensitivity and retain potentially informative sequences (odds ratio > 1; Fisher's exact test p < 0.5).

text.text: To estimate the strength of evidence supporting each putative Spike-reactive TCR, we compared the frequency of each candidate clonotype between HLA-matched post-vaccination repertoires and pre-2019 SARS-CoV-2-naïve repertoires.Sequences with odds ratios greater than one were retained.
We then transformed odds ratios using Yule's Q statistic: , 𝑄 = ( 𝑂𝑅 -1 ) / ( 𝑂𝑅 + 1 ) which bounds enrichment estimates between 0 and 1.

The resulting Q value was assigned as a sequence-level confidence weight, with larger values, closer to 1, indicating stronger enrichment in post-vaccination repertoires and therefore greater confidence that the detection of that TCRβ clonotype represents S antigen recognition as opposed to sampling noise or an irrelevant TCRα:TCRβ pairing.
To augment the catalog of statistically inferred clonotypes, we incorporated TCR sequences supported by direct experimental evidence of peptide-HLA binding.

We additionally used longitudinal vaccination studies to identify clonotypes exhibiting evidence of vaccine-induced expansion.
Using paired pre-and post-vaccination repertoires from prior studies 26, 41, 42 , we quantified clonal expansion of individual TCRs following mRNA vaccination.

text.text: Confidence weights for kinetically identified clonotypes were assigned using the same Yule's Q-based framework described above.

Thus, the final catalog was assembled by combining evidence from three complementary sources: (i) statistically inferred HLA-linked Spike-reactive clonotypes, (ii) experimentally validated Spike-reactive TCRs, and (iii) vaccine-responsive clonotypes identified through prior longitudinal repertoire analysis.
When a clonotype was supported by multiple methods, redundant clones were collapsed into a single record linked to the corresponding HLA allele or haplotype.
The resulting catalog contains 7,163 HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCRs annotated with sequence-level confidence weights, which we used to quantify HLA-aware Spike-specific T cell breadth.
Antigen specific breadth is a commonly used metric in TCR sequencing analysis to describe the clonotypic diversity of a T cell recognizing an antigen.
It is the proportion of clonotypes matching a reference catalog divided by the total unique receptor sequence in the sample.
We developed an HLA-aware measure of T cell breadth based on the catalog of HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCRs described above.

Unlike conventional breadth metrics that count all diagnostic SARS-CoV-2-reactive clonotypes equally, this approach restricted breadth estimate to only clonotypes linked to HLA alleles carried by the participant and incorporated sequence-level confidence weights (described above).
For each participant, genotyped HLA alleles were compared against the HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCR catalog.
Catalog entries corresponding to at least one of the participant's HLA alleles were considered eligible matches.
Participant repertoires were then screened for the presence of eligible catalog clonotypes.
Each matched clonotype contributed a sequence-level confidence weight, reflecting the strength of statistical or experimental evidence supporting its Spike specificity.

text.text: Cohort and Participant SelectionCOV-BOOST was a multicentre, randomised, phase 2 trial evaluating third-dose booster vaccination against COVID-19, with a prespecified subgroup undergoing detailed immunological assessments.
We utilized samples collected as part of this trial which was conducted at 18 sites across the UK, encompassing both community and secondary-care settings.
The trial was reviewed and approved by the South Central-Berkshire Research Ethics Committee and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency.
The trial was registered with EudraCT (2021-002175-19) and the Integrated Research Application System (IRAS 299180; REC reference 21/SC/0171).

Participants had previously received two doses of either AstraZeneca ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (ChAd) symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection were evaluated using a calendar-stratified Cox proportional hazards model to account June and November vaccination start months.
Inverse probability weights (IPW) were applied based on case status and vaccine platform to account for the two phase case-control sampling design and recover population-level hazard estimates.
For IPW weighting, participants were grouped by general prime-boost vaccine modalities: (i) Adenovirus / Adenovirus, (ii) . mRNA / mRNA, (ii) Adenovirus / mRNA, (iv) mRNA / Adenovirus, (v) .
Adenovirus / Protein Subunit, (vi) mRNA / Protein Subunit.

The primary endpoint was time to symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection, defined according to the COV-BOOST trial protocol as home antigen test-or PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection accompanied by compatible symptoms.
Follow-up time was calculated from the date of immunologic sampling until the first documented symptomatic infection or censoring.
The primary immunologic variable was HLA-aware Spike-specific T cell breadth (HA-T S ).
Hazard ratios (HRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated using IPW stratified Cox proportional hazards regression.

To evaluate the relative and independent contributions of cellular and humoral immunity, we compared models incorporating HA-T S Breadth, pseudovirus neutralization assay (PNA) neutralization titer 50 (NT50), and IFN-γ ELISpot responses measured at Day 14.

NT50 represents potential antibody-mediated protection, whereas HA-T S Breadth and ELISpot capture complementary aspects of cellular immunity, By comparing nested models containing individual and combined immune correlates, we evaluated whether associations between HLA-aware T cell breadth and infection risk persisted after accounting for humoral immunity and conventional functional T cell response magnitude.
Analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.3 using the survival package (version 3.8).

text.text: Because average DNA yield was higher in earlier batches, which disproportionately contained samples from COVID-19 cases (Extended Data Fig 5 A ), differences in recoverable TCR diversity could potentially confound comparisons of HA-T S breadth between cases and matched controls.
To reduce this potential bias, each sample's repertoire was resampled with replacement to a uniform depth of 100,000 productive templates before computing HA-T[S] breadth (Extended Data Fig 5 B).
Twenty-two samples (18%) yielded fewer than 100,000 productive templates and were designated low-recovery.

Three sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the influence of these samples on the estimated association between HA-TS breadth and risk of symptomatic breakthrough infection: Low-recovery samples were excluded and the primary Cox model refit in the remaining 98 participants (Extended Data Fig 5 C,D model 2), Imputation of low-recovery values.
All participants were retained and Day 14 HA-T S breadth was imputed for low-recovery samples.

A linear regression of Day 14 on Day 0 log2(HA-T S ) breadth was fit in the 98 samples with at least 100,000 productive templates, excluding two near-zero Day 0 breadth values, and used to predict Day 14 values for the low-recovery samples (Extended Data Fig 5 F, G).
Observed values were retained for all other participants.
